{{Short description|Topological construction}}
{{About|topological notion|related algebraic notion|Mapping cylinder (homological algebra)}}
In [[mathematics]], specifically [[algebraic topology]], the '''mapping cylinder'''<ref>{{cite book|last1=Hatcher|first1=Allen|author-link=Allen Hatcher|title=Algebraic topology|url=https://archive.org/details/algebraictopolog00hatc_939|url-access=limited|date=2003|publisher=Cambridge Univ. Pr.|location=Cambridge|isbn=0-521-79540-0|page=[https://archive.org/details/algebraictopolog00hatc_939/page/n10 2]}}</ref> of a [[Continuous function (topology)|continuous]] [[Function (mathematics)|function]] <math>f</math> between [[topological space]]s <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> is the [[Quotient space (topology)|quotient]]
:<math>M_f = (([0,1]\times X) \amalg Y)\,/\,\sim</math>
where the <math>\amalg</math> denotes the [[Disjoint union (topology)|disjoint union]], and ~ is the [[equivalence relation]] [[Equivalence_relation#Generating_equivalence_relations|generated]] by
:<math>(0,x)\sim f(x)\quad\text{for each }x\in X.</math>
That is, the mapping cylinder <math>M_f</math> is obtained by gluing one end of <math>X\times[0,1]</math> to <math>Y</math> via the map <math>f</math>.  Notice that the "top" of the cylinder <math>\{1\}\times X</math> is [[homeomorphic]] to <math>X</math>, while the "bottom" is the space <math>f(X)\subset Y</math>.  It is common to write <math>Mf</math> for <math>M_f</math>, and to use the notation <math>\sqcup_f</math> or <math>\cup_f</math> for the mapping cylinder construction. That is, one writes 
:<math>Mf = ([0,1]\times X) \cup_f Y</math>
with the subscripted cup symbol denoting the equivalence. The mapping cylinder is commonly used to construct the [[mapping cone (topology)|mapping cone]] <math>Cf</math>, obtained by collapsing one end of the cylinder to a point. Mapping cylinders are central to the definition of [[cofibration]]s.

==Basic properties==
The bottom ''Y'' is a [[deformation retract]] of <math>M_f</math>.
The projection <math>M_f \to Y</math> splits (via <math>Y \ni y \mapsto y \in Y \subset M_f</math>), and the deformation retraction <math> R </math> is given by:

:<math> R: M_f \times I \rightarrow M_f</math>
:<math>([t,x],s) \mapsto [s\cdot t,x], (y, s) \mapsto y</math>

(where points in <math> Y </math> stay fixed because <math>[0,x]=[s\cdot 0,x]</math> for all <math>s</math>).

The map <math>f:X \to Y</math> is a [[homotopy equivalence]] if and only if the "top" <math>\{1\}\times X</math> is a strong deformation retract of <math>M_f</math>.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Hatcher|first1=Allen|title=Algebraic topology|url=https://archive.org/details/algebraictopolog00hatc_939|url-access=limited|date=2003|publisher=Cambridge Univ. Pr.|location=Cambridge|isbn=0-521-79540-0|page=[https://archive.org/details/algebraictopolog00hatc_939/page/n23 15]}}</ref> An explicit formula for the strong deformation retraction can be worked out.<ref>{{cite arXiv|last=Aguado|first=Alex|eprint=1206.1277|title=A Short Note on Mapping Cylinders|date=2012 |class=math.AT}}</ref>

== Examples ==

=== Mapping cylinder of a fiber bundle ===
For a [[fiber bundle]] <math>\pi:P \to X</math> with fiber <math>F</math>, the mapping cylinder
:<math>M_\pi = (([0,1]\times P) \coprod X)/\sim </math>
has the equivalence relation
:<math>
(0,p_{x}) \sim (0, q_{x})
</math>
for <math>p_{x},q_{x} \in F_x</math>. Then, there is a canonical map sending a point
<math>[i, p_{x}, x] \in M_\pi</math> to the point <math>x \in X</math>, giving a fiber bundle
:<math>p:M_\pi \to X</math>
whose fiber is the cone <math>CF_x</math>. To see this, notice the fiber over a point <math>x\in X</math> is the quotient space
:<math>[0,1]\times F_x \coprod \{x\}/\sim </math>
where every point in <math>\{0\}\times F_x</math> is equivalent.

==Interpretation==
The mapping cylinder may be viewed as a way to replace an arbitrary map by an equivalent [[cofibration]], in the following sense:

Given a map <math>f\colon X \to Y</math>, the mapping cylinder is a space <math>M_f</math>, ''together with'' a cofibration <math>\tilde f\colon X \to M_f</math> and a [[surjective]] [[homotopy equivalence]] <math>M_f \to Y</math> (indeed, ''Y'' is a [[deformation retract]] of <math>M_f</math>), such that the [[Function composition|composition]] <math>X \to M_f \to Y</math> equals ''f''.
[[Image:Mapping cylinder.png|right]]

Thus the space ''Y'' gets replaced with a homotopy equivalent space <math>M_f</math>, and the map ''f'' with a lifted map <math>\tilde f</math>. Equivalently, the diagram
:<math>f\colon X \to Y</math>
gets replaced with a diagram
:<math>\tilde f\colon X \to M_f</math>
together with a homotopy equivalence between them.

The construction serves to replace any map of topological spaces by a homotopy equivalent cofibration.

Note that pointwise, a [[cofibration]] is a closed [[Injective function|inclusion]].

==Applications==
Mapping cylinders are quite common homotopical tools. One use of mapping cylinders is to apply theorems concerning inclusions of spaces to general maps, which might not be [[injective]].

Consequently, theorems or techniques (such as [[homology (mathematics)|homology]], [[cohomology]] or [[homotopy theory]]) which are only dependent on the homotopy class of spaces and maps involved may be applied to <math>f\colon X\rightarrow Y</math> with the assumption that <math>X \subset Y</math> and that <math>f</math> is actually the inclusion of a [[Subspace topology|subspace]].

Another, more intuitive appeal of the construction is that it accords with the usual mental image of a function as "sending" points of <math>X</math> to points of <math>Y,</math> and hence of embedding <math>X</math> within <math>Y,</math> despite the fact that the function need not be one-to-one.

===Categorical application and interpretation===
One can use the mapping cylinder to construct [[homotopy colimit]]s:{{Citation needed|date=June 2010}} this follows from the general statement that any [[Category (mathematics)|category]] with all [[Pushout (category theory)|pushout]]s and [[coequalizer]]s has all [[Colimit (category theory)|colimit]]s.  That is, given a diagram, replace the maps by cofibrations (using the mapping cylinder) and then take the ordinary pointwise limit (one must take a bit more care, but mapping cylinders are a component).

Conversely, the mapping cylinder is the [[homotopy pushout]] of the diagram where <math>f\colon X \to Y</math> and <math>\text{id}_X\colon X \to X</math>.

===Mapping telescope===
Given a [[sequence]] of maps

:<math>X_1 \xrightarrow{f_1} X_2 \xrightarrow{f_2} X_3 \to\cdots</math>

the mapping telescope is the homotopical [[direct limit]]. If the maps are all already cofibrations (such as for the [[orthogonal group]]s <math>O(n) \subset O(n+1)</math>), then the direct limit is the union, but in general one must use the mapping telescope. The mapping telescope is a sequence of mapping cylinders, joined end-to-end. The picture of the construction looks like a stack of increasingly large cylinders, like a telescope.

Formally, one defines it as
:<math>\Bigl(\coprod_i [0,1] \times X_i\Bigr) / ((0,x_i) \sim (1,f_i(x_i))).</math>
